desc:
The array arr is sorted in strictly increasing order. Its first element is 1 and every other element is a distinct prime number. For every pair of positions i < j consider the fraction arr[i] / arr[j] (a value strictly between 0 and 1).

Sort all n(n-1)/2 fractions by value and return the k-th smallest as the two-element array [arr[i], arr[j]] (numerator, denominator). Because 1 and the primes are pairwise coprime, all these fractions are distinct, so the answer is unique.

Example: for arr = [1, 2, 3, 5] the fractions in order are 1/5, 1/3, 2/5, 1/2, 3/5, 2/3, so k = 3 gives [2, 5].
constraints: arr[0] = 1 and every other arr[i] is a prime number, 2 ≤ arr[1] < arr[2] < ... ≤ 30,000
hints: Putting all roughly two million fractions in a sorted structure works for tiny inputs but is wasteful. Search over the fraction's value, a real number between 0 and 1.

For a threshold t, count the pairs with arr[i] / arr[j] ≤ t. For each numerator index i the matching j form a suffix, and the starting point of that suffix only moves right as i grows, so two pointers count in O(n).

Binary search t in (0, 1). During each count, also remember the largest fraction found that is ≤ t. As soon as the count equals exactly k, that remembered fraction is the answer. Distinct fractions differ by at least about 10-9, so doubles are precise enough.
editorial: For a threshold t in (0, 1), the fractions at most t are counted with two pointers. For numerator index i, let j be the smallest index with arr[i] / arr[j] ≤ t; then all indices from j to n - 1 work. Since arr[i] grows with i, a larger denominator is needed, so j never moves left. While counting we also track the largest qualifying fraction.

Bisect on t: if the count is below k raise the lower bound, if above, lower the upper bound, and when the count is exactly k the largest tracked fraction is the k-th smallest. Termination is guaranteed because all fractions are distinct: there is a gap between consecutive fractions of at least 1 / (30000 · 30000), about 1.1·10-9, which is much larger than double rounding error, so some midpoint isolates exactly k fractions.

Each count costs O(n); about 30-40 bisection steps are needed, for O(n log(1/eps)) time and O(1) space. A min-heap of the next fraction in each row gives O(k log n) instead, which is too slow when k is around n2/2.
